Let $C = C_1\cup C_2$ be a piecewise smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. 

For line integrals with respect to $x,$ we have the following properties:

- $\displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x$

- $\displaystyle\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x + \int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x$

In our case, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 8 & =-{\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 8 & =-(-2)-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 8 & =2-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 6 & =-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_{-C_2} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x = -6.
$$

The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t)+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

v:
Remember that $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ gives the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along $C\mathbin{:}$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r <                                 0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $\mathbf F$ works with the particle for $x >        0,$ while $\mathbf F$  works against the particle for $x <           0.$ 

![](images/67/673798bb131da05a07b3f47894340cbbc143fa6a248823bcfbdf6b5a5238efb4.png)

 
By symmetry, the contribution to $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ for $x <                 0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $x > 0.$ So, 

$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r =     0.
$$

- Statement III is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $\mathbf F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/24/24884d31b2b9aa8d94b11bccfaab1fa31e62a34f4e5183676c79390923f1f243.png)

 
So, $\displaystyle\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r =      0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r <                               0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/06/063836a4780ecb4be6e8c6149a422e3c8e9f2770304e659a8116691b91e3d7f1.png)

So, $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $\mathbf F$ remains unchanged.

![](images/70/704915d2852e1654aa31d17bd2dfb07a3022fe3d8b597f37bf98bd5af2de1d1b.png)

So, $\displaystyle\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is false, while statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/20/20121d30445c9e756f1c2c024713bc6cd6f0464cfcfc24df68bc30c766c4988e.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

- Statement ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/0f/0ff98536c275458d68deabda91f56bf63e7c8f59f5ea79c68292332d8cd58d4f.png)

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$; ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ only.

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

where $\mathbf r (t)$ for $a\leq t\leq b$ is a parametrization of $C.$ 

Now, if we set $f(x,y) = 1,$ then by the change of variables formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the $x$-coordinates at the initial and terminal points of $C,$ respectively. To summarize,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1.
$$

The initial point is $(0,2)$ and the terminal point is $(2,0).$ So, we have $x_1 = 0, x_2 = 2,$ and therefore,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = 2-0 = 2.
$$

Given a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and a path $C$ defined by $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ the line integral 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r
$$

gives the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from the initial point $\mathbf{r}(a)$ to the terminal point $\mathbf{r}(b)$ on the curve.

Now suppose that $C$ is a *closed* curve. The **circulation** of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C,$ denoted using the Greek letter $\Gamma$ (pronounced "gamma"), is given by the line integral

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Remember that the notation $\displaystyle\oint$ simply reminds us that we're integrating along a closed path.

The circulation $\Gamma$ gives the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along the entire closed path. We can also think of $\Gamma$ as a measure of how much $\mathbf F$ circulates around $C.$

Let's build some intuition by considering some examples. 

- Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction, shown below. 

![](images/9e/9e9de4e3734be4f7d8f59f6d54d0ed92c51db3a0beb8277f4b450531b7dab332.png)

It's clear from the picture that $\mathbf{F}$ *assists* the motion of a particle as it moves counterclockwise along the path. Therefore, we can conclude that

$$
\Gamma = \displaystyle\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r >    0.
$$

- Now imagine that $C$ is traversed in the clockwise direction.

![](images/16/16dd701d51e3b43714b58993f66e42359289f557ef86fd9091ab6b8bba7041e7.png)

We see that $\mathbf F$ works *against* the particle's motion as it moves clockwise along the path. Therefore,

$$
\Gamma = \displaystyle\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

- Finally, consider the vector field $\mathbf{G}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the clockwise direction, shown below.

![](images/8b/8bf269cecceeefc3e81b868a4fc4c54127f00432145782b24719bb49552868c7.png)

Since the force $\mathbf G$ acts perpendicular to the particle's motion as it moves around the path, it neither helps nor hinders its motion. Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\Gamma = \displaystyle\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf G\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.
$$

In some situations, a particle's speed increases and then decreases (or vice-versa) as it moves along a curve in a vector field. 

Let's consider a particle moving from $A$ to $B$ along the arc of a semicircle centered at $O$ in a uniform gravitational field, as shown below.

![](images/46/466bd1716e626f6e3cc7859589974c27d49bdaa77bed9aa5813ef4bd9f3328e9.png)

 

Note that:

- as the particle moves from $A$ to $T,$ it works against $\mathbf F$ and slows down, and

- as the particle moves from $T$ to $B,$ it works with $\mathbf F$ and speeds up.

By symmetry, the contribution to $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ for $x <                   0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $x > 0.$ So, 

$$
\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r =     0.
$$

Intuitively, this means that the particle's speed is the same at the points $A$ and $B,$ and these are the points of maximum speed. 

Additionally, since $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ is decreasing as we move from $A$ to $T,$ the particle moves at its slowest speed at the point $T.$

If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

How can we calculate the integral of a sum of functions, like $\displaystyle \int (x+x^3)\,\textrm d x?$ 

According to the **sum rule**, the integral of the sum of functions is equal to the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\int (f(x) \pm g(x))\,\textrm d x = \int f(x) \,\textrm d x \pm \int g(x) \,\textrm d x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x+{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1})+(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+({c}_{1}+{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where we renamed $c_1+c_2=C.$ (The sum of two arbitrary constants is itself an arbitrary constant.)

Suppose that we want to calculate $\displaystyle \int 2x e^{x^2}\,\textrm d x.$

Notice that if we let $u = x^2,$ then both $u$ and its derivative $u'=2x$ appear in the integrand:

$$
\int \underbrace{2x}_{u'} e^{\overbrace{x^2}^u}\,\textrm d x
$$

Integrals like this can always be solved using substitution.

Let $u=x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u = 2x\,\textrm d x.
$$

We now substitute our expressions into the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\underbrace{2x\,\text{d}x}_{\text{d}u} \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, where the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is given by $\mu_{X|y}.$ In other words,

$$
\textrm{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] = \mu_{X|y}.
$$

The **conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as

$$
\textrm{Var}[X\,|\,Y] = \textrm{E}\big[(X - \mu_{X|y} \big)^2 \,|\, Y=y].
$$

As with the discrete case, this definition can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\displaystyle \textrm{E}\big[X^2 \,| \, Y=y \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 \, f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, y) \: \textrm{d}x,
$$

 

and $f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$ Note that these formulas are analogous to those for $\textrm{Var}[X]$ for continuous $X.$

When we select a particular value of $y,$ the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ returns a real number. However, if $y$ is not specified, then $\textrm {Var}[X | Y = y]$ gives us a *function* of $y.$

We have an analogous definition for the **conditional variance of $Y$ given  $X=x{:}$**

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

where 

- $\mu_{Y|x} = \textrm{E}\big[Y \,| \, X=x \big]$ is the conditional expected value of $Y$ given  $X=x,$

- $\displaystyle \textrm{E}\big[Y^2 \,| \, X=x \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y^2 \, f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, x) \: \textrm{d}y,$ and

- $f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$

For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

In our case, for the function $f(x) = \dfrac{k}{(4x+1)^3}$ on the interval $x \geq 0,$ the second condition states that

$$
\int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{k}{(4x+1)^3} \, \textrm dx = 1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{k}{(4x+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =-{[\frac{k}{8(4x+1)^{2}}]}_{0}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{k}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
\dfrac{k}{8} = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = 8.
$$

For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for $x \geq 3,$ we have $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{(x-2)^2} \geq 0.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }(x-2)^{-2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{x-2}\,{|}_{3}^{\infty } \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, the first and second conditions are satisfied. So, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

- Statement ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is true. Indeed,

$$

For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

In our case, for the function $f(x)=k{e}^{-3x}$ on the interval $0\le x<\infty ,$ the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }k{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }k{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x={[-\frac{k}{3}{e}^{-3x}]}_{0}^{\infty }=\frac{k}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
\frac{k}{3}=1\,⟹\,k=3.
$$

v:
Consider the function $f(x)$, defined as

$$
f(x)=\sqrt{\sin x}
$$

A sketch of this function is shown below.

![](images/b1/b1fd56fbb40743ccf15288f79b5847bbd990a239ce8a2cb4fa7f1974d914edc3.png)

The finite area $\mathcal A$ bounded by $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [0,\pi]$ is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin x} \: \textrm{d}x
$$

Let's use our graphing calculator to approximate this area. Since the function we want to integrate contains trigonometric functions, your calculator *must* be in radians mode!

We bring up the definite integral option on most calculators in one of the following ways:

1. Using the $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\displaystyle\color{gray}\,\displaystyle \int_{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}^{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big \mid 0\big \mid}}\,}$ button. You may need to press $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,2\text{nd}\,}$ (or $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{shift}\,}$) first.
2. Using the $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{math}\,}$ (or $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{calc}\,}$) button and selecting the "integration" option. Note that this might be called $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{fnInt}\,}$ or similar.

The next steps depend on whether your calculator uses derivative or function notation. We'll discuss both. You're encouraged to read both instructions as there are several parallels.

Integral Notation

If your calculator uses derivative notation, you should see a prompt that looks similar to the following:

$$
\int_{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}^{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big \mid 0\big \mid}} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}
$$

In this case, we fill in the empty boxes as follows:

- Enter $0$ for the lower integration limit. Then, press $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,}$ to move the cursor to the upper integration limit, and enter the value $\pi$.The prompt should now look as follows:
$\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\pi} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big \mid 0\big \mid}} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}$
- Navigate the cursor to the next empty box by pressing $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,}$. Enter the function definition by pressing the following keys:
$\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\sqrt{\phantom{0}}} \quad\:\: \bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\sin\,}\quad\:\: \bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}X,T,\theta,n} \quad\:\: \bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}$
The prompt should now look as follows:
$\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin(x)} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}$
- Navigate the cursor to the next empty box by pressing $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,}$. Press $\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}X,T,\theta,n}$ to enter the variable that we're integrating with respect to.The prompt should now look as follows:
$\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin(x)} \,\textrm{d}x$
- Finally, press $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\textrm{enter}\,}$, and the calculator will return the numerical value of the integral.

Following the above steps, we obtain

$$
\int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin x} \: \textrm{d}x\approx 2.396
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Function Notation

If your calculator uses function notation, then instead of being presented with

$$
\int_{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}^{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big \mid 0\big \mid}} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}
$$

you'll instead see a prompt that looks similar to the following:

$$
\text{integral}\Big(\bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big \mid}\text{expression}\phantom{\Big \mid}}, \bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big \mid}\text{variable}\phantom{\Big \mid}}, \bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big \mid}\text{lowerBound}\phantom{\Big \mid}}, \bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big \mid}\text{upperBound}\phantom{\Big \mid}}\Big)
$$

In this case, we place the function definition in the first box, the variable in the second box, and the lower and upper limits in the third and fourth boxes, respectively.

By entering this information, the prompt will look as follows:

$$
\text{integral}\Big(\,\sqrt{\sin x}\,, \,x\,, \,0\,, \,\pi\, \Big)
$$

Once you're done, press $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\textrm{enter}\,}$.

Following the above steps, we obtain

$$
\int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin x} \: \textrm{d}x\approx 2.396
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

**Watch Out!**

- It's important to remember that the graphing calculator finds a numerical *approximation* of the definite integral.
- Moreover, different calculators use different algorithms to arrive at their approximations.
- For that reason, different calculators may give slightly different answers when approximating the definite integral of a function.
- Despite this, the answers returned by different calculators will agree when the answer is rounded to two or three decimal places in most cases.

We've seen how to approximate definite integrals using a graphing calculator. In this lesson, we'll apply the techniques we've learned to approximate improper integrals.

Suppose we wish to evaluate the following improper integral to three decimal places:

$$
\int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x
$$

Your graphing calculator is unlikely to include an $\infty$ button, so we cannot directly enter this improper integral into our graphing calculator.

However, recall that, by definition

$$
\int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x = \lim\limits_{a\to\infty} \int_1^a \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x
$$

So instead, let's consider the definite integral

$$
\int_1^a \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x
$$

We now use our graphing calculator to approximate the above integral for increasing values of $a{:}$

- Setting $a=9$, we have
$\displaystyle \int_1^9 \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.170$
rounded to $3$ decimal places.
- Setting $a=99$, we have
$\displaystyle \int_1^{99} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171$
rounded to $3$ decimal places.
- Setting $a=999$, we have
$\displaystyle \int_1^{999} \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171$
rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Since the integrals with upper limits $99$ and $999$ both give $0.171$ to $3$ decimal places, we conclude that

$$
\int_1^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{\ln{x}}}{x^4}\,\textrm d x \approx 0.171
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Recall that the **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

It is common for the set $S$ of a continuous random variable $X$ to be an infinite interval. Therefore, we often need to evaluate improper integrals when determining whether a function is a valid pdf and to compute probabilities associated with such a random variable.

For example, let's consider the following function:

$$
f(x) = {\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{e}^{- x} , \hspace{1em} & x > 0 , \\ 0 , \hspace{1em} & \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right. }
$$

Is $f(x)$ a valid probability density function? Let's start by sketching its graph:

![](images/35/3559a998491a004c159683aaf0946bb4fdf87f4afe873fdc93235e840b4b0ac8.png)

Clearly, $f(x)\geq 0$ for all $x,$ so this function satisfies the first condition.

To check that $f(x)$ satisfies the second condition, we need to compute the following integral:

$$
\int_S f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,\textrm d x
$$

Calculating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & ={[-{e}^{-x}]}_{0}^{\infty } \\  & =[-{e}^{-\infty }]-[-{e}^{0}] \\  & =0-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $f(x)$ satisfies both conditions, we conclude that $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Recall that the **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

The probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

This probability can be interpreted as the area bounded between $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [a,b],$ as shown below.

![](images/e6/e6c21e69a0dbd15ce32d18c2e74d8fcab0276e82bc55b354eaa5140adff610e6.png)

Also, remember that for continuous random variables, we get the same answer whether or not we include the endpoints of an interval $[a,b].$ In other words,

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X < b)  = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b).
$$

In this lesson, we'll get some practice at computing probabilities with continuous random variables.

If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

- The flux $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

First, notice that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0,
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, we know the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s,
$$

where $C_2$ is the straight line from $A(5,3)$ to $B(1,3)$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](images/2a/2aeb26e58251923821d4058f886eada6a29b473ea70714b32e98c5338ddd0b28.png)

Notice that both $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ are $90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C_2,$ we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{C_2} P\,\textrm{d}y - Q\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parametrizing $C_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\,i+3\,j+t\cdot [(i+3\,j)-(5\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(5-4t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=3\sqrt{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\sqrt{(5-x)^{3}}=\sqrt{(5-(5-4t))^{3}}=8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-4t)=-4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3\sqrt{3})\cdot (0)-(8\sqrt{{t}^{3}})\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{64{t}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\left(\frac{64(1)^{5/2}}{5}\right)-\left(\frac{(64(0)^{5/2}}{5}\right) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1\, \textrm{d}s = \dfrac{64}{5}.
$$

$$
\overline{x} = \dfrac{M_O}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $\displaystyle m = \int_a^b \lambda (x) \: \textrm{d}x$ is the mass of the rod,

- $\displaystyle M_O = \int_a^b \, x\lambda (x) \: \textrm{d}x$ is the moment of the rod about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$
\lambda (x) = x^3, \qquad 
a=0, \qquad 
b=2.
$$

So,  the moment of the rod about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(32-0) \\  & =\frac{32}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\overline{x}= \dfrac{M_O}{m} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{32}{5}\right)}{4} = \dfrac{8}{5}.
$$

 

Note that this result makes intuitive sense. Since $\lambda$ is an increasing function of $x,$ we would expect the center of mass to be located closer to the right endpoint and further from the left endpoint.

$$
(\overline{x},\overline{y}) = \left( \dfrac{M_y}{m}, \dfrac{M_x}{m} \right),
$$

where

- $\displaystyle M_x = \iint\limits_D y \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- $\displaystyle M_y = \iint\limits_D x \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \:0 \le x \le 1, \: 0 \le y \le x \big\}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\cdot (x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}xy+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{6}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{5}{6}(\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{5}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\overline{y} = \dfrac{M_x}{m} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{5}{24}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{5}{12}.
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-y)=1-1=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/e2/e22757cf7c4e2be17cb71e63c550aa39a10ee1dc5895c63acd5a45f0baa94623.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(1-2t)\,i+(-1+2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=1-2t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1-y=1-(2t-1)=2-2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-2t)\cdot (2)-(2-2t)\cdot (-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-2t)+(2-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}3-4t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot {[3t-2{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\cdot (3-2) \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=2.
$$

$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m}=\frac{8}{6}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

$$
(\overset{―}{x},\overset{―}{y})=(\frac{{M}_{y}}{m},\frac{{M}_{x}}{m}),
$$

where 

- $m={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A$ is the mass of the lamina,

- ${M}_{x}={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A\,$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- ${M}_{y}={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

Since we require the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass, we need to compute the moment about the $x$-axis: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\cdot 4xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4x{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4x{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{4{x}^{7}}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{8}}{6}]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{256}{6}-\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{85}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\overset{―}{y}=\frac{{M}_{x}}{m}=\frac{\left(\frac{85}{2}\right)}{21}=\frac{85}{42}.
$$

$$

- ${M}_{y}={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

Notice that $D$ is a type II plane region:

![](images/78/78f9da3d48727d2cb3c447be0f4050a044c4aabe29179fd31f04cd7b6c66eabd.png)

So, we have 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1-{y}^{2},\,-1\le y\le 1}
$$

and $\lambda (x,y)={y}^{2}.$ 

Since we require the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass, we need to compute the moment about the $y$-axis: 

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{y}}{m}=\frac{\left(\frac{8}{105}\right)}{\left(\frac{4}{15}\right)}=\frac{2}{7}.
$$

Recall that a lamina's *center of mass* is the point $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ where its total mass could be concentrated to give the same total moment about the coordinate axes as the original lamina. 

The center of mass of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ is given by 

$$
(\overline{x},\overline{y}) = \left( \dfrac{M_y}{m}, \dfrac{M_x}{m} \right),
$$

where 

- $\displaystyle m = \iint \limits_D \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the mass of the lamina,

- $\displaystyle M_x = \iint\limits_D y \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A\:$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- $\displaystyle M_y = \iint\limits_D x \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

Remember that if we could place a fulcrum under our lamina at its center of mass, it would balance perfectly.

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by $$ \mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j} $$ which is defined on an open set $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ Recall that a function $\psi(x,y)$ is said to be a **stream function** of $\mathbf F$ if it satisfies $$ P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}. $$ If a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y),$ then $\mathbf{F}$ is called a **source-free vector field**. Source-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below: - *The divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ at any point of $D$ is zero:* $$ \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0 $$ - *The *flux* of $\mathbf{F}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero:* $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0 $$ - *Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that* $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s. $$ Stream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.

Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)={e}^{tx}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=x{e}^{tx}\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}>1$ and choose $[c,d]⊂[1,\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=-\frac{2t{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t\ge 1.$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=|x-t|.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆[0,1],$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R.$ However, the partial derivative

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}={\begin{aligned}-1,\,x>t \\ 1,\,x<t\end{aligned}
$$

does *not* exist whenever $x=t={t}_{0},$ and is therefore not defined everywhere on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{tx}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$; ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\ge 1$ only.

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

v:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-8)\,\text{d}x & =-8\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =-8\int {x}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =-8\cdot x+C \\  & =-8x+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1}.$

![](images/ea/ea5ff670f03d0bffb84f0929d19b94bca62f23677f913c01e8e0949d144bc60a.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}c(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}c(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[cxy+\frac{c{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(cx+\frac{c}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(cx+\frac{c}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{c{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{cx}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{c}{2}+\frac{c}{2} \\  & =c\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
c=1.
$$

$$

$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $({x}^{2}+9)(x-3),$ and we get

$$
{x}^{2}+x+42=(Ax+B)(x-3)+C({x}^{2}+9).
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=-2,B=-5,$ and $C=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+x+42}{({x}^{2}+9)(x-3)}=-\frac{2x+5}{{x}^{2}+9}+\frac{3}{x-3}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x+42}{({x}^{2}+9)(x-3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2x+5}{{x}^{2}+9}+\frac{3}{x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+9}\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+9}\text{d}x+3\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use a substitution $u={x}^{2}+9.$ Then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{1}{u}\right)\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+9| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+9).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right),$ which results in

$$

v:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{5}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{2}{5}\int 1\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int {y}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{{y}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\cdot y+C \\  & =\frac{2}{5}y+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 6x{e}^{-3x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=6x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-3x}\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We, substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 6x\cdot {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =6x\cdot \left(-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\right)\cdot 6\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2x{e}^{-3x}+2\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6x{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =-2x{e}^{-3x}+2\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2x{e}^{-3x}-\frac{2{e}^{-3x}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we define

$$

$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}))(x)-\int (x)\left(\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}))(x)-\int (x)\left(\frac{3}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3\int \text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-5x-27 & =(2x+B)(x+1)-({x}^{2}+20).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$  into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}-5(0)-27 & =(2(0)+B)(0+1)-({0}^{2}+20) \\ -27 & =B-20 \\ B & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-5x-27}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+20)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x-7}{{x}^{2}+20}-\frac{1}{x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x-7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution ${x}^{2}+20=u.$ Then, $2x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ and we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+20).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x & =7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+(2\sqrt{5})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =7\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{5}}\right) \\  & =\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{10}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-5x-27}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+20)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+20)-\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{10}\right)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-9x+5 & =(Ax+B)(x-4)+C({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=-1,$ and $C=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{2}-9x+5}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-4)} & =\frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{x-4}\end{aligned}
$$

v:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution.  Let $u={x}^{2}+4$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each integral in turn.

- Statement “${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent” is false. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4))|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As $a\to \infty $, we have that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)\to \infty .$ So the integral diverges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is true. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4))|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{2}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

As $a\to -\infty $, we have that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)\to \infty .$ So the integral diverges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is true. The integral in statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

However, both integrals on the right-hand side are divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

In conclusion,  only statements “${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” and “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” are true.

The position of the particle at $t=5$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,5].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(5)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(1)=2,$ and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{1}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=1$ to $t=5.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t=6.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(5)=2+6=8.
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=5$ is $x=8.$

Line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of parametrization and orientation.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement. 

- Statement ${\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=-4$ is false, while statement ${\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=4$ is true. Reversing the curve's orientation does *not* change the value of a line integral with respect to arc length. Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=4.
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=8,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(u)=⟨16{u}^{4}-12{u}^{2},\,2u⟩$ for $0\le u\le 1.$” is false. Notice that ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ are different parameterizations of the same curve. Since line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of parameterization, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=4.
$$

 
To see that ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ represent the same curve, we can convert each parametrization to Cartesian form. In doing so, we find that both parameterizations give the Cartesian curve

$$
x={y}^{4}-3{y}^{2},\,0\le y\le 2.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=4$ only.

The path $C$ is made up of two parts, as shown below:

![](images/ff/ff52b8e83a9cc9867b25ea3c24ed0f988a27dec73f9e0ab2dfda28ddabb3238a.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path shown above.

Now, we make use of the following facts:

- If $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ is a piecewise-smooth curve, we have

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s.
$$

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $r=4.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\,\text{d}s=\frac{1}{4}(2\pi r)=2\pi .
$$

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle where both legs have a length of $4.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\,\text{d}s=\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=4\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=2\pi +4\sqrt{2}=2(\pi +2\sqrt{2}).
$$

Let $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ be a piecewise smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. 

For line integrals with respect to $y,$ we have the following properties:

- ${\int }_{-C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y=-{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y$

- ${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y$

To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 3x{e}^{-x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-x}\, & ⟹\,v=-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3x\cdot {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =3x\cdot (-{e}^{-x})-\int (-{e}^{-x})\cdot 3\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3x{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =-3x{e}^{-x}+3\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3x{e}^{-x}-3{e}^{-x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

v:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is false, while statement ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/eb/eb4da8143700c7d31e0ceacd09ac76a8d1bcb10379a34dce5b59d48f2ae58c13.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

- Statement ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.

![](images/70/70a473397216589350f63482ab3e36cb1247e7825046c70642254c8514564b00.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ only.

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-3x}\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \left(-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\right)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is true. Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative.

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=1,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is false. $$

{r}_{1}(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [1,e].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}⟨1,\,t⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}1+1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2t\,{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =2(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2(e-1),$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the segment line $\overset{―}{AB},$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$” is false. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨t(e-1)+1,\,t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨1,\,t(e-1)+1⟩\cdot ⟨e-1,\,1⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}e-1+t(e-1)+1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t(e-1)+e\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}(e-1)}{2}+et]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{e-1}{2}+e \\  & =\frac{3e-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is independent of path” is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is path-dependent.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative.

v:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{5}{6},$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is false. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{1}(t)=⟨4t,\,2t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨4{t}^{2},\,-4t⟩\cdot ⟨4,\,2⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}16{t}^{2}-8t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\,{\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{[\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =8[\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{16}{3},$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is true. Parameterizing the curve, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t⟩,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}⟨{t}^{2},\,-{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,\,1⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{3}}{3})-0 \\  & =8-\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is independent of path” is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is path-dependent.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative.

v:
The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(u\,i-2\,j-2\,k)\cdot (4\,i-2\,j+\,k) \\  & =4u+4-2 \\  & =4u+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ we must have $4u+2=0,$ which means that $u=-\frac{1}{2}.$

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot |{e}^{t}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot ({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t]\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t$ using integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⇒ & v={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}x & =t{e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi [{(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})|}_{0}^{1}-{(t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t})|}_{0}^{1}] \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{2}+1-0)-(e-e)+(0-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-3] \\  & =({e}^{2}+2e-6)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's examine each of the given integrals.

- Integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{3}-8}\,$ is not an improper integral since it has finite limits and the function under the integral is finite at every point $x\in [0,1].$

- Integral ${\int }_{-2}^{1}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{3}+8}\,$ is an improper integral of the second kind since it has finite limits, and 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}+8}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to (-2)^{+}.
$$

- Integral ${\int }_{-\infty }^{1}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{3}}$ is an improper integral over an *infinite* domain since its lower limit is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{-2}^{1}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{3}+8}\,$ only.

To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 5x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=5x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=5 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 5x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =5x\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\cdot 5\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is false, while statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$  works against the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/2b/2b8ef08638551571caa43150080a8550a0b61ed24eaa7c6da73fe66edd161e8e.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is true. It's clear from the picture below that if we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $B$ to $A.$

![](images/28/28db5c349d3455c58f81da7c181586ba4e0ad5662f35faa2575d6622b3713988.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$; ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ only.

For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement ${\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{x+1}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}([\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+2]-[\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+0]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is true. Since statements “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” and ${\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$”; ${\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$; “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function”.

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $m={\int }_{a}^{b}\lambda (x)\,\text{d}x$ is the mass of the rod,

- ${M}_{O}={\int }_{a}^{b}\,x\lambda (x)\,\text{d}x$ is the moment of the rod about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$
\lambda (x)=\sqrt{x},\,a=0,\,b=4.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {4}^{3/2}-0 \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the moment of the rod about the origin is

$$

$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m}=\frac{\left(\frac{64}{5}\right)}{\left(\frac{16}{3}\right)}=\frac{12}{5}.
$$

$$
(\overset{―}{x},\overset{―}{y})=(\frac{{M}_{y}}{m},\frac{{M}_{x}}{m}),
$$

where 

- $m={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A$ is the mass of the lamina,

- ${M}_{x}={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A\,$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- ${M}_{y}={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

Notice that $D$ is a type I plane region:

$$

and $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\cdot [y]_{y=0}^{y={x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\cdot {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{y}}{m}=\frac{3}{2}.

Improper Integrals

v:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

Let's evaluate each integral in turn.

- Statement “${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent” is false. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi x+1)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{5\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi x+1){|}_{0}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }{lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi a+1)-\operatorname{sin}⁡1].\end{aligned}
$$

As $a\to \infty $, $\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi a+1)$ oscillates between $-1$ and $1.$ So the integral diverges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is true. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi x+1)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{5\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi x+1){|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{sin}⁡1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi x+1)].\end{aligned}
$$

As $a\to -\infty $, $\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi x+1)$ oscillates between $-1$ and $1.$ So the integral diverges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is true. The integral in statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

However, both integrals on the right-hand side are divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

In conclusion,  only statements “${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” and “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” are true.

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$

$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}-\int \frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$

The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i+u\,j-\frac{\pi }{4}\,k)\cdot (\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}\,i+\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}+u-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8} \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ we must have $u=0.$

v:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence.

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and every $s>a,$

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ converges for every $s>a.$” is true. Since $f$ is of exponential order and is piecewise continuous, there exist constants $K,T>0$ and $a$ such that

$$
|f(t)|\le K{e}^{at},\,t>T.
$$

When computing the Laplace transform, we multiply $f(t)$ by ${e}^{-st}.$ If $s>a$, then for all sufficiently large $t$,

$$
|{e}^{-st}f(t)|\le K{e}^{-(s-a)t}.
$$

Because $s-a>0$, the function ${e}^{-(s-a)t}$ is integrable on $[T,\infty )$, and
$f$ is bounded on $[0,T].$
Therefore, the entire integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt
$$

converges.

- Statement “If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform $F(s)$ exists for all $s>a.$” is true. The standard existence theorem for the Laplace transform says that if $f$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and of exponential order $a,$ then the improper integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt
$$

converges for every $s>a.$ This is exactly what it means for $F(s)$ to exist for all $s>a.$

- Statement “The Laplace transform of any piecewise continuous function of exponential order is infinitely differentiable in its region of convergence” is true. The smoothness theorem guarantees

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}
$$

for every $n\ge 0$ and each $s>a,$ which shows that $F(s)$ is infinitely differentiable, even if $f(t)$ itself is not.

Therefore, the answer is “If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ converges for every $s>a.$”; “If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform $F(s)$ exists for all $s>a.$”; “The Laplace transform of any piecewise continuous function of exponential order is infinitely differentiable in its region of convergence”.

Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{|x-t|}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is undefined when $x=t,$ since the denominator vanishes. Thus, ${f}_{1}$ is not continuous on $R,$ and differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{x}{1+{t}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=-\frac{2tx}{(1+{t}^{2})^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+x+t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊂(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=-\frac{1}{(1+x+t)^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (0,1).$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$; ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+x+t}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$ only.

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=\frac{x}{(x-t)^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t<0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$; ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{x-t}\,\text{d}x,\,t<0$ only.
