For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=11,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is convergent}$

- For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

- For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$

$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=11$ is $F(s)=\frac{11}{s},$ defined for $s>0.$

\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

v:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4{x}^{2}+3\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+3)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(-(4{\pi }^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +8\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +8\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡0+8(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+8\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =(4{\pi }^{2}+3-8)-(-3+8) \\  & =4{\pi }^{2}-5-5 \\  & =4{\pi }^{2}-10\end{aligned}
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{5}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{5{ln}^{4}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}.\end{aligned}

Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{3x})(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(3{e}^{3x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\frac{3}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{3x})(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-\int (-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(3{e}^{3x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{3}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\frac{3}{2}J \\ I & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\frac{3}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{3}{2}I) \\ I & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{9}{4}I \\ \frac{13}{4}I & ={e}^{3x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ I & =\frac{1}{13}{e}^{3x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{1}{13}{e}^{3x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{13}{e}^{3(\pi /2)}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )))-(\frac{1}{13}{e}^{3(0)}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{1}{13}{e}^{3\pi /2}(2\cdot 0+3\cdot (-1))-\frac{3}{13} \\  & =-\frac{3}{13}({e}^{3\pi /2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})\,(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2I) \\ I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-4x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{10}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
x(7)=x(3)+{\int }_{3}^{7}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(3)=3$, and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{3}^{7}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=3$ to $t=7.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{3}^{7}v(t)\,\text{d}t=8.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(7)=3+8=11.
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=7$ is $x=11.$

Let's denote the indefinite integral by  $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-x})\,(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-\int (-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-x})\,(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =-{e}^{-x}(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(-\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}(0-2))-(-\frac{1}{5}(0+2)) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(1+{e}^{-\pi /2}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-x})(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))-\int (\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =({e}^{-x})(-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))-\int (-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{9}I \\ 10I & ={e}^{-x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{10}(0-(-1)))-(\frac{1}{10}(0-1)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{10}+\frac{1}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}({e}^{-\pi }+1).\end{aligned}
$$

v:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{2}\,g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the adjacent intervals rule and substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the sum rule for definite integrals and substituting the known values, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 18-10 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 4 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x=4.$

$$

- Integral ${\int }_{-\infty }^{-4}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}-9}\,$ is an improper integral over an *infinite* domain since its lower limit is infinite.

- Integral ${\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}}$ is not an improper integral since it has finite limits and the function under the integral is finite at every point $x\in [1,3].$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}-9}\,$ only.

Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3J \\ I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3(-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3I) \\ I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-9I \\ 10I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\left(\frac{{e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{10}\right){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2\pi )}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ))}{10}-\frac{{e}^{3(0)}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))}{10} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{6\pi }}{10}-\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}({e}^{6\pi }-1)\end{aligned}
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2({e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2(\pi /2)}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))+\frac{{e}^{-2(-\pi /2)}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =-\frac{2{e}^{-\pi }}{5}-\frac{2{e}^{\pi }}{5} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}({e}^{\pi }+{e}^{-\pi })\end{aligned}
$$

v:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=5{x}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(5{x}^{2}+1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=10D.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }5{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-(5{\pi }^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +10\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +10\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(-(5(0)^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡0))-10\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0-10\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =5{\pi }^{2}+1-10+1-10 \\  & =5{\pi }^{2}-18\end{aligned}
$$

v:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}z & =\frac{1}{3}\int 1\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {z}^{0}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{{z}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot z+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}z+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

We notice that:  

- the limits for the variable $x$ are from $0$ to $\sqrt{2}$, and

- the limits for the variable $y$ are from $-\sqrt{3}$ to $2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

$$
{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{2}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x.
$$

So, the correct answer is ${∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ $={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{2}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$; ${∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ $={\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$ only.

v:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

v:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution.  Let $u={x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{-u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each integral in turn.

- Statement “${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent” is true. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }({-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}|}_{0}^{a}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-{e}^{-{a}^{2}}+{e}^{0}) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the integral converges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is false. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(-{e}^{0}+{e}^{-{a}^{2}}) \\  & =-1+0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the integral converges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is false. The integral in statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1-1=0.
$$

So the integral converges.

In conclusion, only statement “${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent” is true.

The position of the particle at $t=6$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,6].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(6)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(0)=-2$, and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=0$ to $t=6.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t=9.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(6)=-2+9=7
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=6$ is $x=7.$

Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I) \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2\pi }}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-\frac{{e}^{2(0)}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{2{e}^{2\pi }}{5}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}({e}^{2\pi }+1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3J \\ I & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3({e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3I) \\ I & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-9I \\ 10I & ={e}^{3x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3\pi }}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-\frac{{e}^{3(0)}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3\pi }}{10}+\frac{1}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}({e}^{3\pi }+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)-\int \left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}(\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\left(-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}\right){|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}))}{10}+\frac{{e}^{-0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0))}{10} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{-\pi /3}}{10}+\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}({e}^{-\pi /3}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the constant $A.$ Multiplying both sides of the given equality by $({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+3 & =(Ax+1)(x-1)+{x}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2$  into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2}+2+3 & =(A(2)+1)(2-1)+{2}^{2}+4 \\ 9 & =2A+1+8 \\ 9 & =2A+9 \\ A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{0x+1}{{x}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right).\end{aligned}

$$
\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|.

The position of the particle at $t=7$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,7].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(7)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{7}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(1)=4,$ and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{1}^{7}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=1$ to $t=7.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{1}^{7}v(t)\,\text{d}t=-3.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(7)=4+(-3)=1
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=7$ is $x=1.$

Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡((-x)^{2}) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+1)$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x+1) \\  & =-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(1-x) \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{3}-2x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{3}-2(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}+2x \\  & =-({x}^{3}-2x) \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({x}^{3}-2x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{-5}^{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x$; ${\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({x}^{3}-2x)\,\text{d}x$ only.

$$

$$

$$

v:
Recall that, if $F=P\,\text{i}+Q\,\text{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

* $F$ is a source-free vector field.

* $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

* The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

* Flux is path-independent. That is, given two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and end points, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

* There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, for our vector field $F=({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{i}-2xy\,\text{j}$, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy) \\  & =2x-2x \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero. Hence,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (2x+1){e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x+1\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{3x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (2x+1)\cdot {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =(2x+1)\cdot \frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}-\int \frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2x+1){e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{(2x+1){e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(2x+1){e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{2{e}^{3x}}{9}+C \\  & =\frac{(6x+1){e}^{3x}}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$

For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{0}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is true. Since statements “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” and ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$”; ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$; “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function”.

For the first integral, we have

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[2\sqrt{x-5}]}_{6}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2\sqrt{6-5}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3}\,{x}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{x}^{1/3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\sqrt[3]{a}-1) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1+\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =1,\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{4}{k}=1\,⟹\,k=4.
$$

Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)=-2+2=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/21/212435c94989d0553db86b8d39edae3a7905d41ef668bb33fa0a62bed99d5462.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(-1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-2x=1-2(-1)=3, \\ Q(x,y) & =2y=2(2t-1)=4t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)=0, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=6.
$$

For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{1}^{2}]-[{0}^{2}] \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is true. Since statements “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” and ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$”; ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$; “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function”.

We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=12{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 12{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}(4{x}^{3})-\int (4{x}^{3})\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}+\frac{8{x}^{3}}{9}-8D \\  & ={x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})]}_{1/2}^{e/2} \\  & =[{\left(\frac{e}{2}\right)}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & \,-[{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{8}{9})]-[\frac{1}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4-\frac{8}{3}+\frac{8}{9})]-\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{9} \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3}-2}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x(6)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(1)=2$, and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{1}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=1$ to $t=6.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{1}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(6)=2+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{7}{2}.
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=6$ is $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=2{x}^{4}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2(-x)^{4} \\  & =2{x}^{4} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(-x)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-6x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x) \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $f(x)=3{e}^{-x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =3{e}^{-(-x)} \\  & =3{e}^{x} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the correct answer is ${\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x$ only.

Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(u-1)^{3}}\,\text{d}u & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{(u-1)^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2(u-1)^{2}}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{2(a-1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{2(2-1)^{2}}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2(a-1)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{z}^{3}]}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{a}^{3}) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{a}^{-2} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integral ${\int }_{-\infty }^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z$ is divergent.

For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

In our case, for the function $f(x)=k{e}^{-8x}$ on the interval $0<x<\infty ,$ the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }k{e}^{-8x}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$

For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\ge 1$” is true. Indeed, for $x\ge 1,$ we have $f(x)=\frac{7}{{x}^{8}}\ge 0.$

- Statement ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{7}{{x}^{8}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{7}}\,{|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is true. Since statements “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\ge 1$” and ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ are true, the first and second conditions are satisfied. So, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\ge 1$”; ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$; “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function”.

Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Hence, the correct answer is ${\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x$; ${\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ only.

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is false, while statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works against the particle for $x>0,$ while $F$  works with the particle for $x<0.$ 

![](images/af/af80eab6427f376084301c03715fd098cfe4a1c816dcd72d3e1129cfa35ff29d.png)

 

By symmetry, the contribution to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $x<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $x>0.$ So,

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/a2/a26ca79400bf30aa891543d30a052a6e8ec071ccb48fcd8c418fe0a713dad212.png)

 

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ only.

v:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is true. Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative.

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=e,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is true. Since $F$ is conservative, there exists a function $f$ such that $∇f=F.$ Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,\frac{\pi }{2})-f(0,0) \\  & ={e}^{1}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-{e}^{0}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =e\cdot 1-0 \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\frac{\pi }{2}\sqrt{x},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” is false. Since $F$ is conservative and ${C}_{2}$ has the same initial and terminal points as ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=e.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$F$ is conservative”; “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=e,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$” only.

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is true. Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{y}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative.

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=8,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x),$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$” is true. Since $F$ is conservative, there exists a function $f$ such that $∇f=F.$ Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f=x{e}^{y}.
$$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(3,\operatorname{ln}⁡3)-f(1,0) \\  & =3\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-1\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =3\cdot 3-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=3,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$” is false. Since $F$ is conservative and ${C}_{2}$ has the same initial and terminal points as ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=8.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$F$ is conservative”; “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=8,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x),$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$” only.

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is true, while statement ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves clockwise along $C.$ 

![](images/b2/b2473eb0c505d75d2c448c1a0d714d05d42737ce8d601401e925834a25ae9e14.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- Statement ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves counterclockwise along $C.$

![](images/85/8513d9d15d204b6f63f310a37465d6b8dfb21239ca412bac7d3b9936f2bf5ebf.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$; ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ only.

The center of mass of a rod placed along the $x$-axis over the interval $a\le x\le b$ whose mass density function is $\lambda (x)$ is given by 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $m={\int }_{a}^{b}\lambda (x)\,\text{d}x$ is the mass of the rod,

- ${M}_{O}={\int }_{a}^{b}\,x\lambda (x)\,\text{d}x$ is the moment of the rod about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$
\lambda (x)=6{x}^{2}+1,\,a=0,\,b=1.
$$

So, the mass of the rod is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}+x]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the moment of the rod about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot (6{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{3}+x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne 0,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ traversed from $A$ to $B$ in counterclockwise direction” is true. Parameterizing the curve, we have

$$
{r}_{1}(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}1\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\pi  \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the segment line $\overset{―}{AB},$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$” is true. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨0,\,1-2t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨2t-1,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-2⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is independent of path” is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is path-dependent.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative.

The center of mass of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda (x,y)$ is given by 

$$
(\overset{―}{x},\overset{―}{y})=(\frac{{M}_{y}}{m},\frac{{M}_{x}}{m}),
$$

where 

- $m={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A$ is the mass of the lamina,

- ${M}_{x}={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A\,$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- ${M}_{y}={∬}_{D}x\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

Notice that $D$ is a type I plane region:

![](images/e6/e6027dcb30cf0d638dc4472c40182ddf9bd85d52840d1268d00c4d3ecbc09abc.png)

So, we have 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \frac{4}{x}}
$$

and $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{1}{x}.$ 

Since we require the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass, we need to compute the moment about the $x$-axis: 

$$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={y}^{2}-2\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =({y}^{2}-2)\left(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}\right)(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=y\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(y)\left(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}\right)(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$

We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(2{x}^{2})(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$  We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+4\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4D \\  & =2((2-{x}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=4D.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(2{x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =(2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D) \\  & =(2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+4x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-4D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[(2{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+4x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =((2{\pi }^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +4\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(1\operatorname{sin}⁡0+4(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0-4\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(0-4\pi -0)-0 \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y)=2-2=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/6b/6bb6e38f83006fa9874ca0020e4eb016ea8eed7fec79596e984b94a0f3853d75.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(-3t+2)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2x+y=2(-3t+2)+(2t-1)=-4t+3, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2y=-2(2t-1)=-4t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t+2)=-3, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t+3)\cdot (2)-(-4t+2)\cdot (-3)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-8t+6)+(6-12t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12-20t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[12t-10{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(12-10) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=2.
$$

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+2x{y}^{2}\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2x{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement $∇\cdot F=0$ is false. Indeed, we have that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+4xy=2x(1+2y)\ne 0.
$$

- Statement “There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F$” is false, while statement “There exists a close curve $C$ such that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s\ne 0$” is true. Indeed, they follow from the fact that $∇\cdot F\ne 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “There exists a close curve $C$ such that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s\ne 0$” only.

v:
The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(4\,i-j+u\,k)\cdot (\frac{e}{2}\,i+3e\,j-k) \\  & =2e-3e-u \\  & =-e-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${\int }_{1}^{3}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ we must have $-e-u=0,$ which means that $u=-e.$

v:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/63/6371bb04d33719ee18c65a92354e84be0e9077e780eac9559dcb7ec42deb8d99.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.

![](images/0b/0bd9476fa9b19f04b40fbb9cca2986ed90495aa134307606622ef91070af19a7.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

v:
The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi }c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i+u\,j)\cdot (2\pi \,i+\pi \,j+(2-\pi )\,k) \\  & =2\pi +u\cdot \pi +0\cdot (2-\pi ) \\  & =\pi (2+u).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${\int }_{0}^{\pi }c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ we must have $\pi (2+u)=0,$ which means that $u=-2.$

To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x-{x}^{2}\le y\le x\le 1\}.$

![](images/c7/c7e555ed139343a1a83e0b05bdb9a13be502271b76e9b9bbdf7ed5f3e869fcd0.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x-{x}^{2}}^{x}c\sqrt{x-y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x-{x}^{2}}^{x}c\sqrt{x-y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}c[{\int }_{x-{x}^{2}}^{x}c\sqrt{x-y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}c{[-\frac{2}{3}(x-y)^{3/2}]}_{y=x-{x}^{2}}^{y=x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}c(-0+\frac{2}{3}(x-x+{x}^{2})^{3/2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2c{x}^{3}}{3}dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2c{x}^{3}}{3}dx & ={[\frac{c{x}^{4}}{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{c}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{c}{6}=1\,⇒\,c=6.
$$

To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

Let's check the above conditions for each of the given functions.

- The function $f$  is *not* a valid probability density function because it does not satisfy the second condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{1}^{e}4xy\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}[{\int }_{1}^{e}4xy\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{[2{x}^{2}y]}_{x=1}^{x=e}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}2({e}^{2}-1)y\,\text{d}y \\  & =[({e}^{2}-1){y}^{2}]_{1}^{e} \\  & =({e}^{2}-1)^{2} \\  & \ne 1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g$ is *not* a valid probability density function because it does not satisfy the first condition. For example,

$$
g(1,e)=\frac{2-e}{4e}≱0.\,\times 
$$

- The function $h$ is a valid probability density function. Indeed, we have $h(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$  and

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{R}^{2}}h(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}h(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}[{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{[\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{y}]}_{x=1}^{x=e}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{1}^{e} \\  & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$h$ only."
