To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y<1-x\le 1\}.$

![](images/ab/ab6a4fce220150c53a70ca236843203460a7040cc1a1b5dfe664c6d45dd93ac1.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}c\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1-x}c\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[cy]}_{y=0}^{y=1-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}c(1-x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c(1-x)\,\text{d}x & ={[-\frac{c(1-x)^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{c}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{c}{2}=1\,⇒\,c=2.
$$

Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[2\sqrt{x-1}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-1}-2\sqrt{2-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-1}-2) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|a|) \\  & =-\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{1}) \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integrals ${\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\,\text{d}x$ and ${\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x$ are divergent.

To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2-y\}.$

![](images/72/7280ccde2bcdd9fab928ddff23dc0da5e48c75920ddd1ce2566dcb1c113a226e.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-y}cx{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating  $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{y}^{2-y}cx{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{c}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x=y}^{x=2-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{c{y}^{2}}{2}((2-y)^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{c{y}^{2}}{2}(4-4y+{y}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{c}{2}(4{y}^{2}-4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2c({y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}2c({y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y & =2c{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2c[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}] \\  & =\frac{c}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{c}{6}=1\,⇒\,c=6.
$$

v:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves clockwise along $C.$ 

![](images/f8/f87d2e735ad58e0b33a813fb91ab202ac0eeaf90575979ea45f954fb7e1d0493.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement III is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves counterclockwise along $C.$

![](images/10/102c11f9002e29a3759679c6ff0bd10188908d33eb9cc94a84d900956adc33a5.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero.
Hence,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-8x-4y))=4-4=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/36/363ebd04d2629ed2b1b29ccab326e22737cf42e4c026d62910a50a1dd88e80f2.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(2-3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4x+2y=4(2-3t)+2(1-2t)=-16t+10, \\ Q(x,y) & =-8x-4y=-8(2-3t)-4(1-2t)=32t-20.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-3t)=-3, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-16t+10)\cdot (-2)-(32t-20)\cdot (-3)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(32t-20)+(96t-60)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}128t-80\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[64{t}^{2}-80t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =64-80 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-16.
$$

$$

We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{2}\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int {x}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot x+C \\  & =\sqrt{2}x+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

From the fundamental theorem of calculus, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(3)-f(-3) \\ {\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(3)-\left(-\frac{5\pi }{2}\right) \\ f(3) & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

The definite integral of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ over $[-3,3]$ is the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis. The corresponding region is a semicircle, so we find the area using the formula 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi \cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x=A=\frac{9\pi }{2}.$ 

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3) & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+\frac{9\pi }{2} \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of parametrization and orientation.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement. 

- Statement ${\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=-k$ is false. Reversing the curve's orientation does *not* change the value of a line integral with respect to arc length. Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=k.
$$

- Statement ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=\frac{2k}{5}$ is false, while statement ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=k$ is true. Notice that ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ are different parameterizations of the same curve. Since line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of parameterization, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=k.
$$

 
To see that ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ represent the same curve, we can convert each parametrization to Cartesian form. In doing so, we find that both parameterizations give the Cartesian curve

$$
x=\sqrt{{y}^{2}+7},\,0\le y\le 3.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=k$ only.

$$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works with the particle for $y<0,$ while $F$  works against the particle for $y>0.$ 

![](images/53/537aca6190fc2f3e06e85c0781a8bb461559ef0a7515ee29aca505f9d615f820.png)

 

By symmetry, the contribution to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $y<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $y>0.$ So,

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/49/4939f9a22400a7a56eaeacb77d520e522f50aa8378ca1014a19810122e12da51.png)

 

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)\left(\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {log}_{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡x)(x)-\int (x)\left(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D) \\  & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2x{log}_{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{x{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{2D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+2)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2) \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2}{{ln}^{2}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{e-2}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(1)dx \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =({\pi }^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -(({0}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0-2\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =({\pi }^{2}+1)\cdot 0+2\pi (-1)-2\cdot 0-0 \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}

$$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true while statement II is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy)=2x-2x=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,1)$ to $B(5,4)$ and  ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](images/18/18b1a5bdc11ca3c2b4b728cf8df3a3e1c4b6c2fbbe86549e9ad773367495c533.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+j+t\cdot [(5\,i+4j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=(4t+1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}+8t+1, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2xy=-2(4t+1)(3t+1)=-24{t}^{2}-14t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((16{t}^{2}+8t+1)\cdot (3)-(-24{t}^{2}-14t-2)\cdot (4))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,144{t}^{2}+80t+11\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[48{t}^{3}+40{t}^{2}+11t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(48+40+11) \\  & =99.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=99.
$$

{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,3)$ to $B(5,3)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](images/3d/3d64ffb0e4cc313a2857d1c20922c1202619d0bdeb3d97f2808b4995c99f7f9f.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+3\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+3\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=-\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=-\sqrt{27}, \\ Q(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}=((4t+1)-1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as $\oint_C F\cdot dr=\oint_C(5 x y^{2})\,dx+(5 x + e^{\cos{(y )}})\,dy$.

Green's theorem states that $\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y})\,dA$.

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/3b/3b1a8cf50ccf8ab3a73f31753def3c2fee2143a7372309cccf2ff7a5e68aedd9.png)

Since $P(x,y)=5 x y^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=5 x + e^{\cos{(y )}}$, we obtain $\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=10 x y$, $\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=5$.

Applying Green's theorem, we get $\oint_C F\cdot dr=\iint_D(5-(10 x y))\,dA=\iint_D(- 10 x y + 5)\,dA$.

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as $\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 3,0\le\theta\le2\pi\}$.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that $\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r\,dr\,d\theta$.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as $\iint_D(- 10 x y + 5)\,dA=\iint_\Delta(- 10 r^{2} \sin{(\theta )} \cos{(\theta )} + 5)r\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{3}r (- 5 r^{2} \sin{(2 \theta )} + 5)\,dr\,d\theta$.

Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is false, while statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion.

![](images/dc/dcc2f364085ccca85e6e6ddd8a5affac51c84f774281b817d4852bd2322bcb1b.png)

So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$.

- Statement ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ the force is still perpendicular to the motion.

![](images/50/508e0ac5f67d7b119ad689ccaede8894268eefe31d9b00f148ddd6bf851de6b4.png)

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$ only.

The path $C$ is made up of two parts, as shown below:

![](images/49/494158fe124fe1c8e1f7f618695dc9846991bd074b199a45a5874ddb8ad16e86.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path shown above.

Now, we make use of the following facts:

- If $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ is a piecewise-smooth curve, we have

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s.
$$

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $r=\frac{34}{3}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\,\text{d}s=\frac{1}{4}(2\pi r)=\frac{17 \pi}{3} .
$$

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle where both legs have a length of $\frac{34}{3}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\,\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\frac{34}{3}}^{2}+{\frac{34}{3}}^{2}}=\frac{34 \sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=\frac{17 \pi}{3}+\frac{34 \sqrt{2}}{3}=\frac{17}{3}(\pi+2\sqrt{2}).
$$

Now, we make use of the following facts:

- If $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ is a piecewise-smooth curve, we have

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s.
$$

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $r=\frac{16}{3}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\,\text{d}s=\frac{1}{4}(2\pi r)=\frac{8 \pi}{3} .
$$

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle where both legs have a length of $\frac{16}{3}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\,\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\frac{16}{3}}^{2}+{\frac{16}{3}}^{2}}=\frac{16 \sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=\frac{8 \pi}{3}+\frac{16 \sqrt{2}}{3}=\frac{8}{3}(\pi+2\sqrt{2}).
$$

v:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int x{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={sec}^{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x-\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ where $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{sec}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\int \frac{1}{u}(-\text{d}u) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

v:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by  $I=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+4I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4({e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+4I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-16I \\ 17I & =-{e}^{-4x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )))-(-\frac{1}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{17}(-1+0)+\frac{1}{17}(1+0) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{17}+\frac{1}{17} \\  & =\frac{1}{17}(1+{e}^{-4\pi }).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-J \\ I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+I) \\ I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I \\ 2I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\left(\frac{{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{2}\right){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi ))}{2} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-\pi }-{e}^{\pi })\end{aligned}
$$

To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{4}{3},\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le 2-y\}.$

![](images/2c/2c984b3c51548a6c9181575cefe27427d12f07c499c4b44fd3fd0bddb0d710af.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{4/3}{\int }_{y/2}^{2-y}cy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating  $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4/3}[{\int }_{y/2}^{2-y}cy\,dx]dy & ={\int }_{0}^{4/3}[cxy]_{x=y/2}^{x=2-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4/3}(cy(2-y)-c\frac{{y}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4/3}(2cy-\frac{3c{y}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4/3}(2cy-\frac{3c{y}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}y & ={[c{y}^{2}-\frac{c{y}^{3}}{2}]}_{0}^{4/3} \\  & =\frac{16c}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{16c}{27}=1\,⇒\,c=\frac{27}{16}.
$$

To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1\}.$

![](images/ea/ea5ff670f03d0bffb84f0929d19b94bca62f23677f913c01e8e0949d144bc60a.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{cx{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{cx}{2}\right)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{cx}{2}\right)\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{c{x}^{2}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{c}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{c}{4}=1\,⇒\,c=4.
$$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4t\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int 4t\,\text{d}t=\frac{4{t}^{2}}{2}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4t(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)^{2}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)}^{2}(2{t}^{2})-\int (2{t}^{2})\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)^{2}-4\int t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/1b/1b22d5486ce7cd4ed083842ba019b454ff711f9fc5b50718b97e58e95ce647ad.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/4f/4f2ae4819d2534d2e6abfbfe4a2842597f1ad0845f7925f5f74c359b69f7ba1f.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{2}⁡(2x))^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡(2x)}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=24{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 24{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=8{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 24{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{2}⁡(2x))}^{2}(8{x}^{3})-\int (8{x}^{3})\left(\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡(2x)}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =8{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{16}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(2x))\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 24{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =8{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{16}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D) \\  & =8{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{16{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(2x)}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{16{x}^{3}}{9{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{8{x}^{3}{ln}^{2}⁡(2x)}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{16{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2}+\frac{16{x}^{3}}{9{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(8{ln}^{2}⁡(2x)-\frac{16}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{16}{9})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{16D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Note that in the above calculation, we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡(2x)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}24{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(8{ln}^{2}⁡(2x)-\frac{16}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{16}{9})]}_{1/2}^{e/2} \\  & =\frac{(e/2)^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(8{ln}^{2}⁡(e)-\frac{16}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)+\frac{16}{9})-\frac{(1/2)^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(8{ln}^{2}⁡(1)-\frac{16}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{16}{9}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}/8}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(8-\frac{16}{3}+\frac{16}{9})-\frac{1/8}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(0-0+\frac{16}{9}) \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3}}{9{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2}{9{ln}^{2}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{1}{9{ln}^{2}⁡2}(\,5{e}^{3}-2\,)\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(4{x}^{2})(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$  We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =4{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D) \\  & =4{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-8\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8D \\  & =4(({x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-8D.$

To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

Let's check the above conditions for each of the given functions.

- The function $f$ is a valid probability density function. Indeed, we have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$  and

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2-xy}{3}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2-xy}{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{4x-{x}^{2}y}{6}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{4-y}{6}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[4y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g$ is *not* a valid probability density function because it does not satisfy the first condition. For example,

$$
g(1,2)=\frac{1-2}{4}=-\frac{1}{4}≱0\,\times
$$

- The function $h$ is a valid probability density function. Indeed, we have $h(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$  and

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{R}^{2}}h(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}h(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{x}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{y}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$f$ and $h$ only."

Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2})$ is an odd function, but integral I is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

- The function $g(x)=x-{x}^{5}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)-(-x)^{5} \\  & =-x-(-{x}^{5}) \\  & =-x+{x}^{5} \\  & =-(x-{x}^{5}) \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}(x-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((-x)^{4}+1) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1) \\  & \ne -h(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

v:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

In our case, for the function $f(x)=k{e}^{x+1}$ on the interval $x\le 1,$ the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}k{e}^{x+1}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}k{e}^{x+1}\,\text{d}x &=k{e}^{x+1}\,{|}_{-\infty }^{1}=k{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
k{e}^{2}=1\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}.
$$

v:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{5x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{3}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3{ln}^{2}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{5x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{5x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{3}⁡x)\left(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{5}\right)-\int \left(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{5}\right)\left(\frac{3{ln}^{2}⁡x}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{5}-3\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{5x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{5}-3I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{5}-3I \\ 4I & =\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{5} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{5x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{20}({ln}^{4}⁡x)\,{|}_{e}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}({ln}^{4}⁡({e}^{2})-{ln}^{4}⁡(e)) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}((2\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{4}-(1\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}({2}^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

v:
Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works against the particle for $y<0,$ while $F$ works with the particle for $y>0.$ 

![](images/30/306fdb7f7a6054d214940d1ca9614c35905f015f34d175561a7850781b751a93.png)

 
By symmetry, the contribution to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $y<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $y>0.$ So, 

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/c9/c9ea0397e7ba2a2ce6aef1058c6935a3282e12df5adc3b3d564cfb87c5f76c3b.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Applying the Integration By Parts Twice

v:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{5}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{5}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=8x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 8x\,\text{d}x=4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 8x({log}_{5}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{5}⁡x)}^{2}(4{x}^{2})-\int (4{x}^{2})\left(\frac{2{log}_{5}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{2}{({log}_{5}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int x{log}_{5}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int x{log}_{5}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{5}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{5}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{5}⁡x)\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{5}⁡x}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{5}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 8x({log}_{5}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =4{x}^{2}{({log}_{5}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{5}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+D) \\  & =4{x}^{2}{({log}_{5}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{4{x}^{2}{log}_{5}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}+C \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{2}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}-\frac{4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}(4{ln}^{2}⁡x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{8D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{5}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}8x({log}_{5}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}(4{ln}^{2}⁡x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}(4{ln}^{2}⁡e-4\operatorname{ln}⁡e+2)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}(4{ln}^{2}⁡1-4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}(4-4+2)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}(0-0+2) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}-\frac{2}{{ln}^{2}⁡5} \\  & =\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡5}(\,2{e}^{2}-2\,)\end{aligned}
$$
